title: Love, then do
hookLine: Augustine: love, and do what you will

lines: ON A POSTER, IT SOUNDS LIKE PERMISSION.
A HARDER RULE THAN ANY LIST.
cards: Love, and do what you will. On a poster, that sounds like permission: follow your heart, do your thing.

But it comes from a sermon by Augustine, bishop of Hippo in North Africa, one of a series he preached on the same short letter from this past week, First John. In its setting it isn't permission at all.
It's closer to a warning, and a harder rule than any list.

teach.b: First, the problem Augustine was looking at: the same outward act can come from opposite places. A father can be stern with his son, and a kidnapper can be gentle with a child he means to sell. Which one loves the boy?
Not the gentle one. He reaches for the Gospel too: the Father handed the Son over, and Judas handed him over. The same verb, says Augustine, but one acted from love and the other from betrayal.
So you can't judge an act by how it looks from outside. Second, the sentence, offered as one short command.
In Latin it runs, dilige, et quod vis fac: love, and do what you will. Third, what comes right after, which the poster leaves off.
If you keep quiet, keep quiet out of love. If you speak up, speak up out of love. If you correct someone, correct out of love.
If you spare someone, spare them out of love. Let the root of love be inside, he says, and from that root nothing but good can grow.
Fourth, why it's harder than a rule. A rule can be kept with a cold heart, every instruction followed out of spite, or pride, or fear.
Augustine moves the test inside, to the root: before the act, is this coming from love? Love first. Then do.
Some readers hear a freedom in that; others hear a very high bar. It may be both.

how: Some Christians who draw on Augustine's teaching examine their motives at the end of the day, asking whether what they did and said came from love.

o: permission to follow your heart and do anything
in Augustine, the root every act should grow from
a list of rules to keep, whatever you feel inside

games.q: inside Augustine's sermon — tap the pairs.
p: may be the one who loves
love, and do what you will

s: Augustine meant: follow your heart and do anything you like
he meant the opposite of a loophole: every act, quiet or loud, must grow from love.
the line comes from Augustine's sermons on First John
it's from his homilies on the letter that says God is love.
Augustine judged acts by how they look from outside
his point is that the same act can come from love or from betrayal.

games.q: you need to correct a friend who's in the wrong. on Augustine's rule, what matters most?
o: say it gently, whatever the reason.
stay quiet to keep the peace.
games.why: if you correct, correct out of love; if you keep quiet, keep quiet out of love. the test is the root, not the tone.

practice: Bring to mind one thing you're about to do today: something you'll say, a correction you need to make, a no you need to give.
Look underneath it, the way Augustine asks: is the root love for the person, or the wish to win, to be right, to be left alone?
You don't have to cancel it; just look, and if the root isn't love yet, see whether the same act could come from love instead, asking for that if you pray.

wordCard.voice: Love. In Augustine's sermon, the root every act should grow from: love, and then do what you will, whether you speak or stay silent. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin, from Augustine's seventh homily on First John: love, and do what you will.

carryVoice: Your line: nothing but good can grow. First the root, then the act. Day eight hundred thirty-four, done.
